st-1.title: Scope rules for every agent carrying this document
st-1.note: The prompt is loaded as system context by the orchestrator and by every sub-agent at every depth, so it opens by disambiguating who owes what. Standards (verification, measurement, safety, reporting) bind universally; side effects (Slack, Drive, spending, cancelling siblings) belong only to whoever's task brief grants them. Without this block a 50-agent swarm would post 50 kickoff messages.

st-3.title: The task, in one sentence
st-3.note: Template slot TASK_TARGET. Fixes the modality (de novo miniprotein binders), the method family (structure-based design-and-filter), and two competing objectives: peak affinity zero-shot AND high hit rate. Optimising only for the top design would satisfy goal 1 and fail goal 2, which is why the deliverable is 30 ranked designs rather than one.

st-5.title: Target dossier and the human comparison arm
st-5.note: Template slot TARGET_DOSSIER: accession, oligomeric state and constitutive cofactor, which downstream sections turn into hard scoring-construct requirements. The competition link is not decoration — it establishes that human expert teams are working the same target, making this a benchmarked head-to-head rather than an open-ended exercise.

st-7.title: Reference access policy and the offline corpus
st-7.note: Every cited source is mirrored in the bundled corpus, so a paywall or dead link is explicitly not an excuse to skip a reference. Names the entry point (_MASTER_SOURCE_INDEX) and warns that large PDFs are page-split. This is the prompt closing the most common agent failure mode: silently dropping an input it could not fetch.

st-9.title: Ref 1 — BenchBB benchmark
st-9.note: Adaptyv's community benchmark for binder design; establishes what hit rates are achievable and how the assay that will score these designs actually works.

st-10.title: Ref 2 — Protein Optimization 101
st-10.note: First of a four-part Adaptyv primer series. Practitioner-level guidance on binder optimisation, included so the agent inherits community craft knowledge rather than reasoning from papers alone.

st-11.title: Ref 3 — Protein Optimization 102
st-11.note: Continuation of the optimisation primer. Relevant to the mandatory in silico optimization rounds specified later.

st-12.title: Ref 4 — Protein Optimization 103
st-12.note: Third part of the primer series.

st-13.title: Ref 5 — Has binder design been solved?
st-13.note: Adaptyv's assessment of the field's current ceiling. Frames how much headroom a campaign like this can expect, and what counts as a good result.

st-14.title: Ref 6 — MBP case study with BindCraft
st-14.note: A worked end-to-end case study on one target. The closest thing in the reference set to a template for the campaign's own workflow.

st-15.title: Ref 7 — Crowdsourced design, EGFR competition preprint
st-15.note: The peer-reviewable write-up of a large crowdsourced binder competition. Supplies measured in vitro outcomes for a wide range of methods against one target.

st-16.title: Ref 8 — EGFR competition round 1 data
st-16.note: ProteinBase collection with per-design sequences and measured binding. Doubles as known-binder corpus material for the novelty gate.

st-17.title: Ref 9 — EGFR competition round 2 data
st-17.note: Second round of the same competition; shows how much the field improved between rounds.

st-18.title: Ref 10 — Agents vs Humans
st-18.note: Directly relevant prior art: an evaluation of whether LLM agents can design proteins competitively with humans. This campaign is a scaled-up instance of that question.

st-19.title: Ref 11 — MUNI hackathon submissions
st-19.note: The underlying per-design data for the agents-vs-humans comparison.

st-20.title: Ref 12 — TREM2 competition
st-20.note: One of the campaign's own 14 targets, previously run as a public competition. Provides both a difficulty prior and known binders to exclude on novelty grounds.

st-21.title: Ref 13 — Myostatin / GDF-8 competition
st-21.note: Prior art for the GDF-8 target, which is the only target in the set carrying a selectivity requirement against a close paralog.

st-22.title: Ref 14 — GEM x Adaptyv RBX1 competition
st-22.note: Competition announcement for RBX1, a zinc-coordinating RING domain — the target that most stresses the cofactor-representation rules below.

st-24.title: Ref 16 — RBX1 all submissions
st-24.note: Full submission set including failures, which is the more informative half for calibrating expected hit rate.

st-25.title: Ref 17 — Nipah-G submissions overview
st-25.note: Editorial overview of the Nipah-G competition submissions.

st-26.title: Ref 18 — Nipah-G competition
st-26.note: Competition page for the Nipah-G attachment glycoprotein target.

st-27.title: Ref 19 — Nipah-G results
st-27.note: Measured binding outcomes for Nipah-G designs.

st-28.title: Ref 20 — Nipah-G all submissions
st-28.note: Complete Nipah-G submission set, hits and misses.

st-29.title: Ref 21 — RFdiffusion re-validation
st-29.note: An independent wet-lab re-run of RFdiffusion designs. Important because it separates published performance from reproducible performance — exactly the distinction the Verification section insists on.

st-30.title: Ref 22 — BindCraft v1 re-validation
st-30.note: The same independent re-validation treatment applied to BindCraft.

st-31.title: Ref 23 — AlphaProteo technical report
st-31.note: DeepMind's binder generator. Cited for its results and filtering strategy; the model itself is not on the roster.

st-32.title: Ref 24 — AlphaProteo blog
st-32.note: Accessible companion to the AlphaProteo report.

st-33.title: Ref 25 — Cao et al. 2022, design from target structure alone
st-33.note: The foundational demonstration that binders can be designed from an unliganded target structure — the premise the whole campaign rests on.

st-34.title: Ref 26 — Watson et al. 2023, RFdiffusion
st-34.note: Method paper for a roster tool that is asterisked, i.e. subject to the 50-backbone-per-target floor.

st-35.title: Ref 27 — Pacesa et al. 2025, BindCraft
st-35.note: Method paper for BindCraft, whose free derivative FreeBindCraft is an asterisked roster tool.

st-36.title: Ref 28 — BoltzGen preprint
st-36.note: Method paper for another asterisked roster generator.

st-37.title: Ref 29 — BoltzGen release designs
st-37.note: The designs shipped with the BoltzGen release, usable both as a performance reference and as novelty-gate material.

st-39.title: Target dossier: the biology gate before any compute
st-39.note: The densest block in the opening. It converts a literature review into machine-checked state: oligomeric state, cofactors, exact assay construct and which PDB depositions represent it. The scoring construct is then frozen per arm at gate time and re-asserted on every production row by parsing the output structure — chain count and cofactor atoms must match /state/gates/{target}.json or the score is written as NaN with CONSTRUCT_FAIL, never a number.

st-41.title: Design against multiple depositions, not one
st-41.note: Guards against overfitting a single crystal form. Priority goes to the structure matching the assay construct, with cross-checks against the others where affordable. Explicitly separates apo/holo conformational questions (handled by the dossier) from oligomer-modelling questions (handled at scoring).

st-43.title: Epitope selection policy
st-43.note: Prefers epitopes with design precedent and a plausible mechanism of action over novel ones, but permits novelty given a stated hypothesis. Cross-species reactivity is explicitly demoted to a secondary objective that may never cost primary affinity or hit rate — a guard against an agent optimising a metric nobody asked to maximise.

st-45.title: Licence boundary on tooling
st-45.note: Any open-source tool with a commercially available licence is in scope; anything else is out. This one sentence is what later excludes AlphaFold3 weights, Rosetta/PyRosetta and ESM3 despite all three being obvious choices technically.

st-47.title: The roster is examples, not an allowlist
st-47.note: Framing line. 'In no particular order' plus 'examples' keeps the list from being read as exhaustive — additions are governed by the rule at line 61, not by this list.

st-49.title: Structure design / co-design roster
st-49.note: Thirteen generators. The asterisk is load-bearing: it marks the seven methods subject to the 50-backbone-per-target floor enforced by the DISPATCH agent. The parenthetical also records that HalluDesign and Protein Hunter are wrappers that hallucinate through a co-folding backbone, so they inherit that backbone's dependencies.

st-50.title: FoldCraft install notes and why it is on the roster
st-50.note: Names the exact repository, records that it does not need PyRosetta (which would put it out of licence scope), and pre-empts two known install failures. The strategic reason for its inclusion: it can produce beta-containing and mixed alpha/beta folds, which is how the 10% non-all-alpha diversity target at line 69 gets met.

st-51.title: Sequence design roster
st-51.note: Only two named tools, both soluble-optimised variants. The base variants are permitted for backbone search but not for designs that get ordered — solubility liability is a wet-lab failure mode the campaign cannot measure in silico.

st-52.title: The three-arm scoring instrument, and its substitutes
st-52.note: Splits co-folders into three tiers: the frozen three-arm ranking instrument (bring up first), substitute-only supplements usable when an arm fails on a target, and AF_Unmasked as diagnostic only. The tiering is what makes 'the instrument' a stable object that can be frozen and disclosed rather than drifting per design.

st-53.title: ESMFold2 install and inference recipe
st-53.note: Pins weights, warns that the PyPI 'esm' package is a different project, and freezes inference parameters so scores are comparable across the campaign. Declares both variants instrument backbones: failure to run them is a halt-and-post condition, not a degrade-and-continue. Also fences the pre-AF3 folder set to AlphaFold2/Multimer and reproductions.

st-54.title: Protenix v2 recipe, and the hardest bring-up gate in the prompt
st-54.note: Exact pip pin, CUDA base, checkpoint source, CLI invocation and the flags NOT to pass. Then the operational trap: the first call JIT-compiles a CUDA kernel for 4-6 minutes, so TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR must live on a shared persistent volume and the first canary needs a 15-minute timeout. Production generation and scoring on every target is held until this reaches roster PASS; five failed fresh-H100 attempts is a halt.

st-55.title: AlphaFold3 engine with OpenFold3 weights
st-55.note: The licence workaround: AF3's JAX code paired with open OF3 weights is fully Apache-2.0, where AF3's own weights are not. Positioned as a permissive cross-check, explicitly not allowed to displace the frozen instrument.

st-57.title: TOOL-BRINGUP stage and the sandbox-termination contract
st-57.note: Budgets the first hour to one sub-agent per roster tool plus ipSAE, MMseqs2 and DockQ, each proving a canary and leaving a run_<tool>.py on the shared volume. Then two cost invariants: every direct Sandbox.create wraps termination in try/finally, and host.compute jobs are terminated by the per-10-jobs monitor in the same cycle they are harvested. Includes the counter-intuitive rule that a non-zero exit with declared output present is a HARVEST, not a re-run.

st-59.title: Structure-to-sequence adapters must be validated too
st-59.note: A specific, experience-shaped warning: generators emit CA-only PDBs, non-standard residue comp_ids and swapped chain order, all of which break sequence design silently. The instruction is to validate the adapter on a campaign target, not the tool in isolation — testing components separately is how this class of bug survives to production.

st-61.title: Adding tools, and the three named exclusions
st-61.note: New tools may join once a production agent has run them end to end on a real target; unrun or licence-unconfirmed tools are out of scope and the correct response is a logged deviation, not shipping dependent designs. Names the three exclusions on licence grounds: AlphaFold3 weights, Rosetta/PyRosetta, ESM3.

st-63.title: What counts as a design
st-63.note: Defines the deliverable object: single-chain miniproteins of 50-120 residues, 35-160 permitted with recorded rationale. The absolute rule is that everything is generated de novo — no known miniprotein, peptide, nanobody or antibody may be used as a starting point or graft. That is what makes the campaign a test of generative design rather than of optimisation.

st-65.title: Method floor: 50 backbones per asterisked method per target
st-65.note: The prompt's main anti-monoculture device. DISPATCH recomputes the (target, method) count matrix every 15-minute cycle, writes it to /state/floor_matrix.json — a missing matrix is itself a deviation — and prioritises under-represented cells. Throughput, cost and skill availability are explicitly rejected as grounds to skip a method. Above the floor, reallocation toward what works is encouraged. Note the single-dispatch-owner invariant: exactly one submit-token issuer, and the orchestrator never calls submit_gate itself.

st-67.title: Target-fold mimic failure mode
st-67.note: A generator conditioned on a full oligomeric complex, asked for a binder about the length of one protomer, will often just reproduce that protomer — because in the training data a protomer genuinely is an excellent binder of its neighbours. Named here as a design-time hazard; caught mechanically by the TM-score branch of the novelty gate at line 81.

st-69.title: Fold diversity target: 10% non-all-alpha
st-69.note: Defined operationally via DSSP (one beta strand of 3+ consecutive E/B residues, or helical fraction below 70%) so it can be computed rather than judged. Deliberately a reported target, not a ranking gate: if the pool cannot supply it without displacing better designs, ship fewer and state the count and reason. An example of the prompt choosing disclosure over a hard constraint.

st-71.title: Sequence design protocol
st-71.note: Soluble variants for anything headed for order; base variants fine for search. Caliby must run both fixed-backbone and over a 32-structure Protpardelle-1c ensemble per its own paper. Co-design models get scored on both their native sequence and a redesign, and cross-pipeline mixing is encouraged for diversity.

st-73.title: LCP: a mandatory sequence-design restraint
st-73.note: Local Composition Perplexity penalises homopolymer stretches per-position. Notable as the one place the prompt requires implementing a method from a figure rather than a paper — the definition lives in Figure 1, shared with permission, and lcp_score must be recorded for every sequence designed.

st-75.title: Figure 1 caption — LCP definition
st-75.note: Attached to the kickoff message rather than embedded in the markdown. The agent must read the figure to implement the penalty; there is no prose fallback.

st-77.title: Figure 2 caption — LCP results
st-77.note: Evidence that the LCP restraint improves sequence design, supplied so the requirement reads as motivated rather than arbitrary.

st-79.title: Pre-scoring filters run before any co-folding spend
st-79.note: Ordering rule with a cost rationale: cheap filters run before expensive GPU scoring. Carefully separates two timelines — UniRef90 staging is not a dispatch gate (production may start without it), but the full novelty check and Ubiquitin rejection must complete before any row reaches the FINAL sheet. Curated mini-databases are explicitly out of scope; it is full UniRef90 or nothing.

st-81.title: Filter 1 — novelty, with three independent thresholds
st-81.note: Checks against UniRef90, the known-binder corpus, and every chain of the target's own reference and control structures. Three rejection criteria: >60% identity over >50% coverage, or >=30% gapped local identity over >=40 residues, or TM-score >=0.5 to any target or control chain. That last one is what catches target-mimic protomers here rather than downstream. Ubiquitin gets a named special case because it emerges with terminal extensions that defeat exact matching.

st-82.title: Filter 2 — developability liabilities
st-82.note: Cysteine parity, homopolymer runs, surface hydrophobic patches. Cheap sequence-level checks for the things that make a protein fail at the CRO rather than in silico.

st-83.title: Filter 3 — monomer foldability
st-83.note: Does the binder fold on its own? Threshold frozen per target at the validation gate, defaulting to mean pLDDT 70. The parenthetical about scale is a real trap: ESMFold2 emits 0-1 where most tools emit 0-100, so a naive threshold comparison would pass everything or nothing.

st-84.title: Filter 4 — structural plausibility
st-84.note: Backbone geometry, clashes, core packing. Thresholds are the agent's to choose but must be frozen at kickoff — the prompt consistently prefers a disclosed arbitrary threshold to a drifting one.

st-86.title: Rejects must be traceably absent downstream
st-86.note: A gate counts as run only when its rejections can be shown missing from every later pool. This closes the gap between a filter that computes a verdict and a filter that actually removes anything — a distinction that is invisible in logs unless someone checks.

st-88.title: Redundancy clustering, with different rules per pool type
st-88.note: De novo pools cluster at ~90% identity before scoring so near-duplicates don't consume GPU budget. Mutagenesis and close-variant pools deliberately skip that — near-identity is the point there — and drop only exact duplicates, deferring diversity enforcement to selection time.

st-90.title: Provenance keys and the frozen method vocabulary
st-90.note: root_backbone_id and structure_method are assigned at backbone generation and propagate unchanged through every downstream stage, which is what makes the per-backbone diversity cap computable. Method names are enum tokens from a campaign-frozen method_vocab.json, not free text, with rfdiffusion and rfdiffusion3 kept distinct. The sheet writer then recomputes every gate from the row's own sequence and structure and admits the row only on agreement to 1e-4 — carried values are never trusted.

st-92.title: Selection caps: six ceilings applied in order
st-92.note: Exact duplicates out, Levenshtein-5 near-neighbours out, then per-backbone 5%, per-TM90-cluster 10%, per-structure-method 50% with at least three methods, per-seq-method two-thirds. Explicitly ceilings and not quotas. The instruction if 30 rows cannot be filled is to fix upstream — generate more, use more methods — rather than relax, with the relaxation ladder deferred to the deliverable spec.

st-94.title: Why these three arms, and the cofactor rule for all of them
st-94.note: Justifies the instrument empirically: the bundled benchmark paper shows the three chosen models match or beat AlphaFold3 as de novo binder filters, especially with multiple distinct seeds at one sample each. Restates the per-arm MSA configuration, then closes a loophole — all three are all-atom co-folders that accept ions, ligands, nucleic acids and modified residues, so a dossier-flagged cofactor is supplied to every arm and 'this arm is protein-only' is never a valid waiver.

st-96.title: The instrument, stated plainly
st-96.note: Three arms, one sample per seed: ESMFold2-Fast single-sequence, ESMFold2-Full with target MSA, Protenix v2 with target MSA. The short block that everything else in the scoring section refers back to.

st-98.title: Two-metric ranking: ipSAE and pose agreement, and the two summary scores
st-98.note: The scoring core. Each arm contributes ipSAE_min and sc_DockQ against the designed complex, using that arm's own argmax-ipSAE seed and best symmetric chain relabelling. pose_dockq is the minimum across arms; three-arm agreement on both metrics is called the strongest in silico evidence available. Two summaries are kept deliberately separate: final_score, the raw mean of six terms, is the headline; rank_zscore, the 4:1 ipSAE:DockQ weighted z-average, is used for ranking only. Both must be frozen and disclosed before production scoring.

st-100.title: Seed-tier structure
st-100.note: Header introducing the two-tier compute strategy: cheap wide screening, expensive narrow confirmation.

st-102.title: SCREEN tier — 1 seed per arm
st-102.note: The wide filter. Ranks on rank_zscore and keeps whatever top fraction the budget supports. Fast iteration is the explicit purpose; nothing at this tier is shippable.

st-103.title: INTERMEDIATE / FINAL tier — 5 distinct seeds per arm
st-103.note: Header for the confirmation tier. 'Distinct' is enforced later by an assertion that the seed set has five unique integers and that per-design variance is non-zero.

st-104.title: Intermediate use is unrestricted
st-104.note: Five-seed scoring may be used freely between waves and optimization rounds. The only thing that distinguishes intermediate from final is which pool it ranks.

st-105.title: FINAL tier and the frozen-mask rule
st-105.note: Spells the ranking formula out term by term: three per-arm ipSAE_min values maxed over seeds and weighted 4, three sc_DockQ values weighted 1. Under a disclosed REDUCED_MASK the raw mean runs over realised terms only and score_instrument names them. The closing sentence is the sharpest in the section — dropping a validated arm from a frozen mask is called sheet corruption, not a judgement call.

st-107.title: Mask freezing and pre-registration of alternatives
st-107.note: The per-target instrument mask freezes at validation-gate time and is enforced by the sheet writer, not by convention. A different ranking formula is permitted only if it demonstrably separates controls better, and only if frozen and disclosed before any production design is scored — a pre-registration requirement borrowed straight from clinical trial practice.

st-109.title: Eleven co-folding considerations
st-109.note: Header for the most technically dense list in the prompt.

st-111.title: Consideration 1 — the validation gate as a file, not a claim
st-111.note: Production scoring is blocked until /state/gates/{target}.json exists with status PASS, and submit_gate() reads that file on every scoring dispatch. The prompt is explicit that a verbal claim, a Slack post or an in-memory variable does not satisfy it. Two conditions: fold recapitulation against a named CA-RMSD threshold, and positive-control separation. If controls exist but separation fails on every instrument, self-authorisation is barred and a three-step remediation ladder applies.

st-112.title: Consideration 2 — control selection, and why antibodies are demoted
st-112.note: Non-antibody controls are preferred because co-folding models systematically underperform on antibody-antigen interfaces, so an antibody control that fails separation is weak evidence rather than a red flag. Published de novo miniprotein binders are excluded outright as separation controls: they were themselves selected by co-folding metrics, so their separation would be circular. A rare piece of explicit reasoning about evaluation bias.

st-113.title: Consideration 3 — MSA caching and per-arm MSA policy
st-113.note: Target-chain MSAs are staged once per target during bring-up into a shared cache that every MSA-consuming arm reads from, rather than re-querying per call. Binder chains are always single-sequence. Positive controls additionally get an MSA on the control-ligand chain. Single-sequence mode for an MSA-capable arm is a per-target deviation requiring evidence and disclosure.

st-114.title: Consideration 4 — rank on ipSAE_min, track ipTM as shadow
st-114.note: ipTM and LIS come free from the same forward pass and are recorded, but never rank. The reason is stated: on multimeric targets whole-complex ipTM is inflated by the native protomer-protomer interfaces, compressing design-vs-control separation. If ipTM is tracked there, it must be a binder-masked variant.

st-115.title: Consideration 5 — z-scores are transductive
st-115.note: Mean and standard deviation depend on the pool, so a z-score is comparable only within its batch — never across targets, waves or campaigns. The mitigation is to store the raw ipSAE_min vector and seed count on every row so any batch can be re-standardised later. Rank with z, report raw.

st-116.title: Consideration 6 — pose self-consistency
st-116.note: The predicted complex must recapitulate the designed epitope, not merely score well. The mechanical form of this requirement is minimal and checkable: pose_dockq non-null on every ranked row.

st-117.title: Consideration 7 — oligomeric targets score at both 1:N and N:N
st-117.note: Template slot OLIGOMER_CLAUSE. Cropping is allowed during design but never during scoring. Both stoichiometries are scored: 1:N feeds rank_zscore, N:N is recorded alongside with binder-binder clash count, and any design whose N:N score collapses must be disclosed. The N:N reference is constructed by applying the target's own Cn symmetry operators to the single designed pose, with the best symmetric relabelling chosen when computing metrics.

st-118.title: Consideration 8 — non-protein context, restated
st-118.note: Repeats the cofactor rule in the scoring context and repeats the specific waiver it forbids. Also flags that co-folding metrics are not comparable across targets — the same fact that makes per-target z-scoring necessary.

st-119.title: Consideration 9 — no templates in production
st-119.note: Template injection is off by default. AF_Unmasked with a target template is available only as a validation-gate diagnostic when nothing else recapitulates the apo target, and is fenced out of the production scoring and pose-check path entirely.

st-120.title: Consideration 10 — check the model before blaming the model
st-120.note: Before recording that a co-folder cannot represent RNA, DNA, a ligand or an oversized chain, read the model's own paper and API rather than the campaign's wrapper around it. A missing wrapper input class is a bring-up bug; an oversized target is handled by a reasonable crop with the model kept in the panel.

st-121.title: Consideration 11 — ipSAE_min defined exactly for multimers
st-121.note: The most specification-like block in the prompt. Cites Dunbrack 2025 for the min-over-both-alignment-directions definition, then specifies the multimer construction: one union-mask call with mask_target as the union of all protomers, n0 and d0 re-derived from the union sizes, explicitly replacing the stock pairwise loop in ipsae.py. The positive control must be measured on the identical construct and pairing. Closes by noting absolute ipSAE compresses with chain count, so cross-target raw comparison is invalid.

st-123.title: Calibration bands: a ceiling from nature, a floor from nonsense
st-123.note: Establishes an absolute reference frame the transductive z-scores cannot provide. Ceiling from native complexes such as Barnase/Barstar; floor from constructed negatives — non-interacting pairs, shuffled binders, cross-pair mismatches. Everything runs at the same seed count, chain construct and ipSAE pairing as the designs. Explicitly raw-score only, since z-scoring a calibration panel would defeat its purpose. Saturation is only considered once top designs reach the ceiling band on the same model.

st-125.title: Sequence feasibility metric
st-125.note: An ESMC log-likelihood or pseudo-perplexity on every ranked design. A cheap orthogonal signal: does this sequence look like a protein to a language model, independent of whether a structure model likes its pose.

st-127.title: In silico optimization: at least five rounds
st-127.note: Three named approaches, of which the middle is the most specific: feed the *predicted* complex — not the original designed structure — back into sequence design, rescore, and repeat while confidence improves, keeping every round under the same root_backbone_id so the diversity caps still bind. Minimum five rounds, continuing while metrics improve. Selection for order draws from all rounds including the original.

st-129.title: Round discipline: no optimising before you have a pool
st-129.note: Round 1 cannot start until a full generation and sequence-design wave is indexed and 1-seed screened, so optimisation never runs on noise. Each round is scored on the same instrument and seed count that ranked its parents. Promotion to 5-seed happens before parent selection. Rows below 5 seeds are ranked below all 5-seed rows with the count disclosed rather than dropped — a deliberate choice of disclosure over deletion.

st-131.title: Nothing computed is discarded
st-131.note: Five enumerated retention classes: exact configuration including weights checksum and image digest, every structure file from every stage and seed, every metric at the level computed, the run manifest linking design to parent to job, and all logs and failure records. The stated rule — if it was computed, it is saved — is what makes the campaign auditable after the fact by someone who was not there.

st-133.title: 30 designs, ordered by someone else
st-133.note: Names the two CROs and the count, then draws a hard line: the agent does not place the order. The wet-lab step stays under human control, which is also what keeps the safety framing at line 264 coherent.

st-135.title: Modal pricing and the governor arithmetic
st-135.note: Publishes the full per-second rate card and instructs verifying it at kickoff. Then derives the campaign's economics: a 4-core/32-GiB H100 box burns about $4.39/h all-in, $10,000 over 24 h is $417/h, so even pace is roughly 95 H100-equivalents and the 150-instance bootstrap cap already runs 1.58x that. max_instances is defined as a formula over the live-fleet-weighted per-sandbox rate, to be re-derived whenever the GPU mix changes.

st-137.title: The governor: the longest single block in the prompt
st-137.note: The complete spend-control system. Bootstrap ramp of 25 instances per cycle to a 150 ceiling on rate-card readings tagged UNCALIBRATED; a four-condition definition of when a metered reading counts as CALIBRATED; billing-dark alerts at T0+90min and hourly after T0+3h. Exactly four authorised writers of governor.json. Enforcement is at the submitter via submit_gate(), whose entire body is wrapped in try/except and returns False on any exception — fail-closed, because a delayed dispatch costs seconds while an ungated H100 costs dollars. Steps (a) through (g) include a dead-man switch on a stale governor file, a live-sandbox count via the Modal SDK with jittered backoff, and a headroom margin to absorb the check-then-create race. The closing clauses forbid private per-pod caps and any 'degraded mode'.

st-139.title: One GPU tier: H100 only
st-139.note: A simplification argued on two grounds. H100 throughput-per-dollar is competitive with cheaper tiers once weight-load and JIT amortise, and a single tier removes both per-method tier selection and the mixed-fleet weighted-rate calculation the governor would otherwise need. A100 is a last resort.

st-141.title: Token accounting formula, and the SQL rule
st-141.note: Claude spend is effectively unlimited, but reporting it is not freeform: fresh input equals input_tokens minus cache_read_tokens, and cache reads are billed at the cache-read rate exactly once. The trap named is double-counting, since input_tokens already includes cache reads. Every posted spend number must come from a server-side SUM executed in the same cell that composes the post — hand arithmetic and client-side row summing are forbidden.

st-143.title: Scale target: 20,000 to 200,000 designs
st-143.note: A one-order-of-magnitude range rather than a number, sized to the budget. Also settles a scope question in advance: optimisation around hits counts as design work inside the campaign, not as something separate that has to be justified.

st-145.title: Design-count ledger, and why it is a tree of files
st-145.note: One JSONL file per writing frame, never a shared file — because Modal volume appends across concurrent sandboxes are not atomic and silently clobber. Defines the coupled gen_screen job as the unit of generation work: generate, filter in-job, write survivors and the n_generated row so the method-floor matrix sees them immediately, then 1-seed screen on all three arms. Chained screens must dispatch immediately; a queued-but-undrained arm is a logged deviation. Generate-only jobs are permitted solely during bring-up.

st-147.title: Ledger semantics, and the generation backlog cap
st-147.note: Fixes the definitions of generated, screened and ranked at kickoff so campaign totals are a single aggregation rather than a matter of interpretation; any redefinition is a deviation with a reconciliation row. Several hard-won operational rules follow: never mv a shared directory while jobs write into it, route appends through the owning singleton after a fresh remount, and treat an empty ledger after a completed scoring wave as fail-loud rather than a zero. Ends with submit_gate step (d2): generation is refused once a target has 200+ generated and more than twice its scored count.

st-149.title: Resources header
st-149.note: Introduces the two-line resource list that the entire budget apparatus exists to manage.

st-151.title: $10,000 of Modal spend
st-151.note: The scalar that everything in the Compute section is derived from, and the one that changes most consequentially in the multi-target variant.

st-152.title: Practically unlimited Claude tokens
st-152.note: The asymmetry that shapes the whole architecture: GPU dollars are scarce and metered, agent tokens are not. It is why the prompt can demand dedicated singleton sub-agents for clock, budget, watchdog and reporting without worrying about their cost.

st-154.title: BUDGET is a standing agent, not a periodic task
st-154.note: Runs the full campaign window on a 15-minute cycle and holds sole ownership of metered reads and governor writes. States the canonical-source rule plainly: the provider's metered per-job cost is authoritative, a rate-card figure is a cross-check only.

st-156.title: The budget is a target to spend, not a ceiling
st-156.note: An inversion of the usual instinct. Under-pace is called a planning failure rather than a saving, with a specific remedy: every hourly cycle while behind must add work until the projection re-enters the band. The asymmetry is quantified — 5% over beats 50% under, but 50% over is also a failure — and under-spend at close-out must be explained in the report. The guard against gaming is explicit: budget goes to productive work, and hitting a number with busywork is a defect.

st-158.title: Scale-up trigger and evidence-weighted target shares
st-158.note: Three consecutive under-pace cycles cause BUDGET to write a /state/WAKE entry carrying a concrete reallocation demand — which targets, which waves, how many dollars — rather than a generic alert. Per-target shares are explicitly not flat: each dossier carries a literature prior_difficulty, blended on every cycle with live observables into /state/target_weights.json, prior-dominated early and data-dominated later. The blend is the agent's to design and disclose. One hard floor: every target gets enough compute for 30 order-ready designs; above that a hard target may take 10x an easy one.

st-160.title: Generation must stay paced with scoring
st-160.note: A generated design that goes unscored is wasted compute, so the two must run at matched rates. Both directions of imbalance are reportable defects: idle GPUs while designs await scoring, and unused concurrency while jobs queue.

st-162.title: Spend tokens freely
st-162.note: A deliberate restatement. The prompt repeats the token-abundance point immediately before the Deliverables section, where the reporting cadence would otherwise look expensive.

st-164.title: Deliverables header
st-164.note: Splits the output into continuous deliverables (Slack, Drive) and final artefacts, both of which follow.

st-166.title: Slack updates
st-166.note: Header for the four-part communication protocol.

st-167.title: Kickoff post: the only top-level message of the campaign
st-167.note: Fixed header format including target, model, date and frame id. Its timestamp becomes the thread anchor: saved as an artifact and passed as thread_ts on every subsequent send. One top-level post per campaign is what keeps concurrent campaigns from colliding in a shared channel.

st-168.title: Morning update at 9:00 AM Eastern
st-168.note: The one scheduled human-facing checkpoint, broadcast out of the thread so it appears in the channel. Content is specified: progress, plan, failures and questions, plus a resource ledger with GPU dollars, token cost, per-target gate status read from the gate file, and progress fraction. 'Including weekends' pre-empts the human assumption that cadence pauses.

st-169.title: Hourly update
st-169.note: Brief in-thread status carrying model name, target, and current best final_score — or best ipSAE_min while no final row exists yet. The fallback matters: the update is required from hour one, before any scoring has produced a rankable row.

st-170.title: Threading invariant: exactly three permitted broadcasts
st-170.note: Every post after kickoff carries thread_ts and reply_broadcast=false. Only the daily morning update, the campaign-conclusion post and a genuine emergency may broadcast. Sub-agents receive the thread_ts in their brief, saved once as an artifact rather than re-derived. A stray broadcast is handled proportionately: acknowledge in the next status block and continue, not halt.

st-171.title: The fixed-format status block
st-171.note: Six mandatory fields. Field (c) carries the sharpest rule: an ESTIMATE-based pace mark must read UNCALIBRATED as its entire pace field, and no pace adjective may accompany it — the prompt refuses to let an uncalibrated number wear the costume of a calibrated one. Field (f) surfaces the deviation count from an append-only JSONL, making deviations visible hourly rather than only at close-out.

st-172.title: Reporting invariant: one function, fresh aggregate, every time
st-172.note: Every number in every Slack post comes from one saved SCRIBE function that runs a fresh server-side aggregate at post time and asserts the truncation flag is false. Memory, cached snapshots, client-side summation over returned rows and output-file counts are all forbidden sources. The stated priority is unusual and deliberate: a fabricated or stale figure is a worse failure than a missing one.

st-173.title: Google Drive deliverables folder
st-173.note: Operator-supplied folder and URL — two of the placeholders that must be filled before launch. Every Drive file must be linked from Slack so the thread stays a complete index.

st-174.title: Drive invariant: one writer, one folder, transactional close-out
st-174.note: Exactly one role may create folders or upload; exactly one campaign sub-folder named for the target; exactly one close_out/ folder whose first file is a README manifest. Close-out is transactional — freeze the ranked sheet, derive every companion from that snapshot, assert the mandatory-non-null columns. A null in a required-but-not-load-bearing column downgrades the row to disclosed-with-deviation rather than dropping it. Uploads happen only after auditor review, because the connector cannot update or delete in place.

st-176.title: Final deliverables header
st-176.note: Introduces the six numbered artefacts that must exist before the campaign can be declared complete.

st-178.title: Deliverable 1 — the design sheet
st-178.note: One CSV, exactly 30 sequences per target and only those 30, with explicit intra-target rank and full metadata. The 'and only those 30' is doing real work: it forbids shipping a longer list and letting the reader pick.

st-179.title: Sheet schema, frozen at kickoff
st-179.note: A schema file written once at kickoff defines column names, dtypes, enums, units and the mandatory-non-null set; per-target writers validate every row against it and the merge script refuses renamed, retyped, missing or duplicated columns. The required-column list is long and deliberately includes provenance (root_backbone_id, parent_design_id, opt_round) and one path column per ranking arm, so every score points at the structure that produced it.

st-180.title: Null policy, rank ordering, and the seed top-up wave
st-180.note: Rank is a single ORDER BY: full-seed status, then pose_PASS, then rank_zscore — the only rank-assignment path in the campaign. Rows below 5 seeds after a failed top-up stay ranked with the count disclosed; the unranked section is reserved for missing or zero scores only. Missing per-arm scores are written as NaN, never as 0.0 or -999 — a sentinel would silently become a real number in any downstream mean. score_instrument records which mask produced the live score so a reader can always tell.

st-181.title: Gate recompute at write time
st-181.note: The writer recomputes every gate from raw inputs at the same threshold the carried flag was set at, and any disagreement is fail-loud and blocks the row. Short, but it is what turns every upstream gate from a promise into a verified fact at the last possible moment.

st-182.title: Companion files header
st-182.note: Introduces the two machine-readable files that make the sheet independently reproducible.

st-183.title: per_seed_metrics.parquet — the sheet's audit trail
st-183.note: One row per design x arm x seed with raw values, so any sheet score can be reproduced without recompute. Coverage must be 100% of ranked design_ids by exact case-sensitive match, and no (design, arm) group may be uniformly null on the ranking metric. Before finalising, 30 sampled rows per target are recomputed from the companion alone and must agree to 1e-4 or the companion is regenerated.

st-184.title: instrument_realization.csv — what the instrument actually was
st-184.note: One row per (target, arm) recording gate status, seeds run, whether the arm fed final_score, control separation, drop reason, and the cofactor and chain-count columns from the dossier rule. Every numeric is DERIVED from the companion and the gate file at write time, never hand-authored, with row-for-row agreement asserted against a recount. This is the table that makes 'we ran the three-arm instrument' checkable rather than assertable, and the report's scoring section is generated from it.

st-185.title: Row count and the relaxation ladder
st-185.note: Exactly 30 ranked rows per target. If gates leave fewer after upstream regeneration has been tried, relax in a fixed order one step at a time, recording on each affected row which step admitted it: diversity caps first with hard stops, then liability flags. pose_dockq and final_score-non-null are never relaxed. Novelty is last resort only, with absolute floors that never move — no two identical rows, no target mimics, no natural-sequence copies. If 30 is still unreachable, ship fewer; padding with duplicates is forbidden. The final sentence forbids implementing relaxation by deleting, commenting out, no-oping or monkeypatching a gate predicate.

st-186.title: Deliverable 2 — the report
st-186.note: A publication-ready PDF in the style of a top-tier Baker-lab paper, with figures and citations. The operative clause is the last one: immediately before declaring it final, every quantitative claim in the abstract and key results is regenerated from the as-shipped artefacts; anything that does not reproduce is corrected and anything untraceable is removed.

st-187.title: Deliverable 3 — the supplement
st-187.note: One archive for everything that does not belong in a PDF.

st-188.title: Supplement contents and path discipline
st-188.note: For every ranked design: the designed complex and every predicted complex used for scoring, in a fixed directory layout keyed by rank and design_id. The sheet's path columns point into this bundle using bundle-relative paths only, deliberately independent of per-job tarballs and Modal workspace paths — so the deliverable stays valid after the compute environment is gone.

st-189.title: ordered_structures is rebuilt from the final sheet
st-189.note: Rebuild is the last close-out step, so the structures cannot drift from the sheet that references them. After rebuild the writer asserts every path column resolves to a real file and that no path embeds a rank prefix disagreeing with the sheet's rank — catching the specific failure where a sheet is re-ranked but the directory names are not.

st-190.title: Retrievability check: open every file, from Drive
st-190.note: Path resolution is not enough — every referenced file must actually open, and from the Drive copy rather than the local one. Below 100% on any target is a defect that blocks close-out. This tests the delivery, not the build.

st-191.title: Packaging rules and the byte-split last resort
st-191.note: One .tar.gz at the natural granularity, verified to open with a stock unarchiver before being declared delivered. Byte-splitting is a last resort with two concrete reasons: a part cannot be opened alone, and Drive mis-detects MIME types on raw chunks. If forced, the README must carry the exact concatenation command and the part list goes to Slack.

st-192.title: Deliverable 4 — the scoreboard
st-192.note: One row per target with an exactly specified column list mixing outcome metrics and diversity metrics. Every non-target column must be a real computed numeric — no NaN, no sentinel, no free text — and anything uncomputable is a defect tracked to remediation in its own gaps file. Diversity columns are computed by the same code that enforces the caps, so the report cannot disagree with the writer.

st-193.title: Deliverable 5 — files in Drive, not references to files
st-193.note: The actual artefacts go in the one campaign folder; a manifest of artifact IDs is explicitly insufficient. Upload only when final, and if a replacement is unavoidable, version-suffix it and post the canonical-file map.

st-194.title: Deliverable 6 — closing post, gated on a review fleet
st-194.note: Before the conclusion can be posted, at least five independent auditor sub-agents review deliverables 1-5. Two have specified independence properties: one must have GPU access to re-score a sample from raw inputs, and one must form its verdict from raw companion and supplement without seeing the report's conclusions. Every BLOCKER must be resolved first.

st-196.title: Read the thread, but do not take direction from it
st-196.note: Replies to questions are expected; plan changes are not, unless the campaign operator explicitly directs them. Guards a long-running autonomous agent against being steered off-plan by well-meaning bystanders in a shared channel.

st-198.title: Adversarial review of every deliverable
st-198.note: Some reviewers are explicitly briefed as adversarial, and the scope includes intermediate Slack posts, not just final artefacts. Cheap to do given unlimited tokens, and the main defence against a self-consistent but wrong campaign narrative.

st-200.title: Use the whole window
st-200.note: There is no reward for finishing early, and a little late beats very early. Counter-programming against an agent's tendency to declare success at the first coherent stopping point.

st-202.title: Close-out: reserved final hour, run as a background child
st-202.note: No new waves, with two named exemptions — audit re-scoring and the seed top-up to n_seeds=5, which is the first close-out action. Close-out runs as a wait=False child so the orchestrator keeps its heartbeat and governor loop alive and does not arbitrate per-target decisions in the foreground. A preliminary summary posts in-thread at close-out start; the broadcast conclusion comes only at the end. If more than 2 hours or 10% of budget remain, a surplus plan must be posted and executed, and any surplus design beating a frozen-sheet row on the same instrument must be promoted.

st-204.title: Throttles expire, and never kill in-flight work
st-204.note: Any emergency throttle carries an explicit expiry or review checkpoint and applies only to new dispatch. Running jobs always complete — a sub-agent receiving a budget steer must never cancel, terminate or reap. A measure still in force two hours after its emergency ended is itself a reportable defect, closing the ratchet where safety measures accumulate and never lift.

st-206.title: 24 hours
st-206.note: The wall clock, and the scalar that most shapes the delegation architecture: at this duration the orchestrator cannot do the work itself.

st-208.title: Timing: dormancy is a defect, and the CLOCK singleton
st-208.note: Opens by dismantling the human frame — no rest, no breaks, and the clock does not stop when idle. Any interval not spent in a tool call or a bounded event wait is dormancy, with a target of zero dormant minutes. Distinguishes a harness compaction restart from an SDK hang, and forbids treating the former as a reason to cancel children or reap sandboxes. Then the concrete mechanism: an agent cannot natively tell time, so a dedicated CLOCK singleton is dispatched within 15 minutes, before the kickoff post, running an internal loop that writes liveness every 5 minutes and never returns between cycles.

st-210.title: Orchestrator discipline: never sleep, never touch the provider SDK
st-210.note: A behavioural specification for the root frame. No time.sleep at any duration; the only permitted parking is wait_for_notification bounded by the next timed obligation. No tool call over ~5 minutes; no foreground collect loops; more than ~5 consecutive waits without an interleaved action is itself a defect. The strongest rule is total: the orchestrator never calls any compute-provider SDK or billing API, not even for diagnostics — all Modal work runs in sub-agents, and its only compute touchpoint is the host.compute submit/result surface. Also fixes the campaign's boot order: dispatch SETUP, block on its return, and dispatch nothing else until it returns OK.

st-212.title: Sub-agents: aggressive swarming on one model
st-212.note: All agents at every depth run the same base model as the orchestrator, so the campaign measures one model's capability rather than an ensemble's. Plan for >50 concurrent work agents at peak. Serial execution of independent methods inside one sub-agent is a reportable deviation. Includes a concrete fallback if the harness refuses a sub-agent's own delegation: the orchestrator dispatches the would-be grandchildren itself as root-level (target x stage) or (target x model) cells.

st-214.title: Delegation: the full agent org chart and its failure detectors
st-214.note: The prompt's architectural centrepiece. A posted delegation architecture in hour one; a quantified failure condition (orchestrator token cost above one third of campaign total after hour 1); four mandatory dedicated singletons. WATCHDOG escalates on heartbeat staleness — stall notice at 15 minutes, ceiling=0 with basis DEAD_ORCHESTRATOR at 30 — and independently brakes a runaway fleet on sandbox count alone, so the halt does not depend on BUDGET being alive or the heartbeat being stale. Singletons are internal while-loops that write liveness unconditionally every cycle; liveness is file age, not frame status, so a kernel reset costs one cycle rather than the chain. Ends with fleet rules: one monitor per 10 jobs, the mandatory out/ copy, the output_file_count<=2 canary-failure rule, and an in-sandbox dead-man switch in the first lines of every run_<tool>.py that self-exits on ceiling=0 or a stale heartbeat — the only control that survives every Claude-side frame being dead.

st-216.title: Literature: re-read on triggers, not on a schedule
st-216.note: Three named triggers, all diagnostic rather than routine: a tool under-producing or failing its gate, a substitution of one instrument for another, and a budget reallocation toward or away from a method. The reasoning is that a config flag or documented limitation usually explains the failure, so reading the paper is cheaper than debugging blind. Each triggered re-read is recorded in the living ideas document.

st-218.title: State only what you have established
st-218.note: The epistemic core. Every factual claim traces to an executed computation or saved artifact; 'verified' means you ran the check and have its output. The last sentence is the most operationally specific in the prompt: no external identifier — DOI, PMID, PDB ID, accession or URL — may be written from memory, ever. Each must be the literal output of a lookup executed in the same session that wrote it.

st-220.title: Anomalies are bugs until investigated
st-220.note: Four named tells, all of which look like success to a careless reader: a score of exactly zero, a gate passing or failing everything, a perfect metric, an impossible runtime. The required response is to halt the affected stage and diagnose, not note and continue. Also extends to inherited inputs — target structures, construct definitions, hotspot numberings — which must be verified against primary sources before anything is built on them.

st-222.title: Cheapest falsifying check first
st-222.note: Before committing significant compute, run the cheapest test that could prove the plan wrong. A seconds-scale sanity check that could kill a multi-hour run always comes first.

st-224.title: Report messy results as messy
st-224.note: One sentence, no elaboration. Permission to be inconclusive, which an agent optimising for a satisfying report would not otherwise take.

st-226.title: Lead with the unfavorable result
st-226.note: Headlines must state the worst defensible reading of the data — not a balanced one. Deviations from the stated method are disclosed, and analyses tuned after seeing results must be declared along with how many configurations were tried. The last clause is a direct guard against garden-of-forking-paths reporting.

st-228.title: Standards bind tighter under autonomy
st-228.note: The justification for everything in the Behavior section. Because no human reviews the work before resources are spent, the agent's own verification discipline is the only gate. Resolves the standing tie-break: when in doubt between a confident result and a flagged uncertainty, flag it.

st-230.title: Roster PASS: five conditions, on a real target
st-230.note: Defines validation operationally. All five must hold on a campaign target rather than a toy peptide, in the same image and flags as production: container builds and imports, weights checksum matches upstream, an end-to-end run of 2-4 designs exits zero, outputs parse as real structures with no NaN coordinates, and the downstream sequence-design adapter consumes one and emits a sequence. Production dispatches exactly that image_id. Also caps commitment — no more than ~10% of budget to any single model until every roster model has passed or been dropped with consequence stated — and requires a canary before any fan-out over 10 jobs. Ends with the reap criterion: terminal status in the ledger, or no output for 2x benchmarked wall-clock; 'looks idle' is explicitly not sufficient.

st-232.title: Your own build is the source of truth; skills are reference only
st-232.note: Defines a build as three things: a pinned image with commit SHAs, weights pulled from the canonical release into a campaign volume, and a run_<tool>.py driver the agent wrote. Then a pointed instruction about the agent's own tooling — a skill's existence is never evidence the tool works in your image, its helpers are never called in production, and where a skill and the upstream README disagree, the README wins.

st-234.title: Verify the first shard before launching the fleet
st-234.note: After the first shard of any scoring or filtering stage, confirm from its outputs — item counts, pass/fail counts, a spot-checked example — that the stage ran as specified. Restates the anomaly rule in gate-specific form: a gate that passes everything, fails everything or returns a constant is broken until investigated.

st-236.title: Pose self-consistency, and the seed-concordance rule
st-236.note: Any ranking model saves its predicted structures, and every scored design gets DockQ plus multiple RMSDs with symmetry-aware chain mapping at full native stoichiometry. The subtle rule: an arm's DockQ is computed on the SAME seed whose ipSAE_min became that arm's score, not on a separately chosen best-DockQ seed — otherwise the two metrics describe different structures. Both argmax seeds are recorded so concordance is auditable. A NaN pose is a missing measurement, not a flag, and blocks rank eligibility. If many top designs are pose_FAIL or the arms disagree, suspect the instrument before the designs.

st-238.title: Validate the exact metric at the exact parameters
st-238.note: If ranking by max over N seeds, validation runs N seeds — not one — demonstrates that the ensemble adds ranking information over a single-seed baseline, and reports measured seed variance. Prevents the common shortcut of validating a cheap proxy and then ranking with something else.

st-240.title: Rank eligibility, seed top-up, and gates as columns
st-240.note: A rank requires the pre-registered protocol or a disclosed relaxation, with the true seed count on every row. Before routing anything to unranked for seed count alone, top-up must be attempted — a design a few seeds short is incomplete, not below protocol. The writer enforces all of this automatically, routes missing-gate rows to unranked with the gate named, and a closing check confirms no ranked row carries an empty or zero score. Diversity caps are called out as a property of the selected set rather than a per-row column, and a gate that exists but was not run is a protocol violation.

st-242.title: Commanded versus delivered counts
st-242.note: Every batch job reports both, and a shortfall over ~10% is a warning in the manifest and updates even when the job exits cleanly. Every count is measured from artefacts or the ledger at write time, never reconstructed from what was commanded; where measured disagrees with planned, report measured and the gap. Bookkeeping writes are idempotent so re-runs cannot double-count.

st-244.title: Liveness watching, the single reaper, and the one-app rule
st-244.note: Five-minute liveness checks, with the specific failure named: a job alive but producing nothing. BUDGET's reap sweep is the sole campaign-wide reaper, bound by the terminal-status criterion, and every terminate must be tag-scoped and cross-checked against the job-metadata ledger. The one-app rule is defensive of others: the workspace has a hard 1000-app cap shared across teams, and a blanket terminate would be destructive against other agents' running work. Closes with the zero-load-bearing-kernel-state rule and a five-step restart sequence, so any gap in activity is recoverable from durable storage.

st-246.title: Final pre-order re-check, and selectivity scoring
st-246.note: Liability, monomer-foldability and diversity are all re-run on the final selected set — assertions rather than trust in upstream. Template slot SELECTIVITY_CLAUSES: for counter-screened targets the ranking formula extends from six terms to nine by adding a per-arm selectivity_delta, defined as on-target minus off-target ipSAE_min computed under the same seed count and aggregation, because an instrument-mismatched subtraction is meaningless. A null off-target or selectivity value on any ranked row is a fail-loud, not a documented gap.

st-248.title: Review fleet independence requirements
st-248.note: At least one reviewer generates new measurements rather than reviewing documents, and at least one forms its verdict from raw data without seeing the conclusions. Every finding ships with the exact query or script that produced each number — review is held to the same traceability standard as the work being reviewed.

st-250.title: Unavailability requires evidence, not inference
st-250.note: Before concluding any tool is unavailable, query HuggingFace, GitHub, PyPI, the skill catalog and the corpus directly. States the reason plainly: several tools named here postdate the model's training cutoff, so 'I have never heard of it' is not evidence of absence. A failed URL is grounds to request network access, and the exact queries are logged with the conclusion.

st-252.title: Logistics: ids, versioning, and secrets
st-252.note: Globally unique design_ids prefixed by target and method; pipeline scripts version-stamped and frozen once production begins, with changes shipping as new versioned copies; script versions and thresholds recorded per design row. Then the security rule: no credential is ever interpolated into a command string, script body, log line, ledger row, artifact or Slack message — secrets reach sandboxes only via modal.Secret or environment injection. A suspected leak is a P0 that stops dispatch from that identity until rotated.

st-254.title: Isolation in a shared account
st-254.note: The channel, the Drive folder and the existing Modal volumes all carry state from other concurrent campaigns, so the agent reconciles only against state it created. The most interesting clause inverts the default suspicion: an unrecognised post in your own thread is by default your own sub-agent's output, and the frames table should be checked before reporting a 'second deployment'. Distinguishes what is reusable infrastructure (prebuilt images, weight volumes) from what is created fresh per campaign, and requires the orchestrator's frame id in every volume name — a date suffix alone is insufficient.

st-256.title: Volume layout: batch to survive the inode cap
st-256.note: One metrics JSONL and one structures tar per job_id, because a 5-seed by 1M-design campaign at one file per design x seed exceeds Modal's inode cap. JIT and torch-extension caches go on the persistent volume. Any delete on a shared volume requires a verified tarball first, and a failed preserve step halts and escalates rather than proceeding.

st-258.title: Slack directives must be verified at source
st-258.note: Any relayed directive is re-read from a fresh thread call with limit >= 500 before acting, and only directives locatable in the thread are acted on. Owner-approved status applies only to a message quoted verbatim with channel and timestamp; sub-agent recommendations, swarm consensus and the agent's own proposals stay labelled as such. A defence against a long agent chain laundering a suggestion into an instruction.

st-260.title: Allocate by evidence; keep a prepared idea list
st-260.note: A target stays active while its best score is still improving or has an untested round remaining, and while untried methods remain. The living ideas document exists so that a stalled target is answered from a prepared, costed, ranked list rather than by inventing under pressure. Each retry must differ from the last in a nameable way, and killing a failing method quickly to redirect its budget is called correct. If wall-clock rather than budget binds, say so and scale concurrency instead of silently cutting planned work.

st-262.title: Autonomy, and the two forbidden calls
st-262.note: No questions and no approval requests for anything within scope and resources, bounded by Claude's Constitution and Anthropic's values. Mechanically: ask_user and ask_about_compute are never called at any depth because both reach the human operator rather than the parent agent; coordination questions route through host.send_message instead. A plan may be posted for tracking but not for approval. Emergency contacts are the three operator placeholders.

st-264.title: Safety: the one section that overrides everything above
st-264.note: Three clauses. Bioterrorism and bioweapons development are absolutely excluded, and the scope is bounded to miniprotein binder design with entirely in vitro validation. Any stop or pause instruction from Anthropic staff, through any channel, is complied with immediately and without debate, explicitly overriding every timeline, budget and perseverance instruction in the document. And the no-questions autonomy rule is carved out: a genuine safety concern means pause and contact the operator rather than resolve it yourself.
